scenes.title: Did this model use my graph data?
cues: Your graph dataset took time to build. Did someone use it to train a model without permission?
TAG Finger investigates this question through black box queries, without accessing the model's training data or parameters.

scenes.title: The training recipe is hidden.
cues: The suspected model may mix your data with other sources, use another learning task, or change its architecture.
A fingerprint tied to one dataset and one task can become unreliable. We need evidence that travels.

scenes.title: Probe behavior. Do not plant a trigger.
cues: TAG Finger leaves the released dataset unchanged. Local text edits are constructed on copies used for audit queries.
The edits act as fingerprints. Ownership evidence comes from the model's response to them, guided by semantics and structure.

scenes.title: Match predictions — and sensitivity.
cues: First, sensitivity guided adversarial knowledge alignment trains a surrogate using the suspected model's output probabilities.
A generator exposes disagreements. The surrogate learns both the prediction distributions and their changes under perturbations.
The suspected model stays frozen. The surrogate becomes the workspace for fingerprint construction.

scenes.title: Keep the text in its graph context.
cues: Next, the surrogate identifies a target node and its most predictively consistent neighbors.
These local regions anchor the text edits in graph structure, rather than editing isolated words everywhere.

scenes.title: Propose. Re-encode. Select.
cues: A language model proposes text edits, conditioned on the region's text, its structure, and a target label.
The same text encoder re-encodes each candidate. The surrogate selects edits that strengthen target responses and regional drift.
Candidate selection alternates with prompt updates. No gradient passes through text generation; this stage does not query the suspected model.

scenes.title: Different tasks. One audit procedure.
cues: Task unified prompts express node, edge, and graph instances as graph or subgraph classification inputs.
Each input receives a learned prompt graph. Task labels remain distinct; only the verification evidence is combined.
This assumes a compatible graph classification interface. It does not transform every arbitrary model API.

scenes.title: A change toward the target is evidence.
cues: Now query the suspected model on clean and edited inputs. Compare the predictions for each task.
A non-target prediction changing to the target gives positive evidence. An unchanged prediction gives zero evidence.
Here, two positive task responses meet the three-task majority threshold and support the dataset-use decision.

scenes.title: No change does not mean no use.
cues: Changes toward another label give negative evidence. If neither side reaches the threshold, the result is uncertain.
One response is not a universal proof. Verification must also be evaluated against models trained without the protected data.
